content_html:
When you owe money on several cards and loans, the order you pay them off in changes how long it takes and how much interest you pay. This calculator lays out the two best-known plans side by side, the debt avalanche and the debt snowball, and compares them with simply paying each minimum, so you can choose an approach with the numbers in front of you.

How to use this calculator

  1. Add your debts: enter a name, the current balance, the APR and the required monthly payment for each one. Use Add a debt for more rows (up to 10) and Remove to delete one.
  2. Extra payment each month: any amount you can pay on top of all the minimums. Even $0 works, because both plans still roll each paid-off debt's payment into the next one.
  3. Read the results: the summary shows the avalanche payoff time and interest, the saving compared with paying only minimums, and the difference between avalanche and snowball. The tables below show the order each debt is cleared and the total balance year by year.

Avalanche vs snowball

Both plans keep your total monthly payment the same from start to finish: the sum of all the minimums plus your extra amount. Every debt gets its minimum, and everything left over goes to one target debt. When the target is paid off, its payment moves on to the next target, so the amount aimed at each new debt keeps growing.

  • Debt avalanche: target the highest APR first. Because the most expensive balance shrinks first, this always costs the least interest (or ties with the snowball).
  • Debt snowball: target the smallest balance first, regardless of rate. You clear whole accounts sooner, which many people find motivating, but you may pay more interest overall.
  • Minimums only: each debt gets its own payment and nothing more. When a debt is paid off, its payment is not reused, so this is the slowest and most expensive option.

The calculation

Each month, interest is added to every open debt at its APR divided by 12. The calculator then pays each minimum (or the remaining balance if that is smaller), applies whatever is left of the monthly budget to the target debts in order, and repeats until everything is paid. Minimum payments are treated as fixed amounts; your card's required minimum may fall as the balance falls, but keeping the payment steady is what makes these plans work.

A worked example

The calculator starts with four debts totaling $21,700: a credit card ($6,500 at 24.99%, $195 minimum), a store card ($1,200 at 29.99%, $45), a car loan ($9,800 at 7.9%, $310) and a personal loan ($4,200 at 13.5%, $145), plus $200 extra a month for a total of $895.

PlanDebt-free inTotal interest
Avalanche29 months$3,960.55
Snowball30 months$4,315.41
Minimums only58 months$7,645.93

Both plans pay off the store card first in month 6, since it has both the highest rate and the smallest balance. After that the avalanche goes after the 24.99% credit card (paid off in month 23), while the snowball turns to the smaller personal loan (month 16) and leaves the expensive card until month 26. That detour costs the snowball $354.86 more in interest and one extra month.

Tips for choosing a plan

  • If the interest difference is small, pick the plan you will stick with. A plan you abandon after three months saves nothing.
  • Stop adding new balances. These plans assume no new charges on the debts being paid off.
  • Keep a small emergency fund. Without one, a surprise expense tends to go straight back on a card.
  • Check for cheaper rates. A lower rate on a large balance, through a consolidation loan or balance transfer, can matter as much as the payoff order.

Results are estimates that assume steady payments and rates. Lenders calculate interest on daily balances, and variable rates can change.

faq.question: Which is better, the debt avalanche or the debt snowball?
faq.answer: The avalanche costs the least interest because it pays down the most expensive debt first. The snowball clears individual accounts sooner, which helps some people stay motivated. If the gap shown in the calculator is small, choose the method you are most likely to follow.

faq.question: What should I enter as the minimum payment?
faq.answer: Use the required payment from each statement. For loans such as a car loan or personal loan, that is the fixed monthly installment. For credit cards, enter the current minimum or the amount you plan to pay each month as a floor.

faq.question: Can I include my mortgage?
faq.answer: You can, but most people leave a mortgage out because its rate is usually low and its term long, so it would be the last debt targeted by either plan. Including it mainly extends the timeline shown.

faq.question: Why do both plans show the same payoff date?
faq.answer: When one debt has both the highest rate and the smallest balance, or when the order of the remaining debts happens to be the same, the two plans attack debts in the same sequence and finish together.

faq.question: Is my information stored or sent anywhere?
faq.answer: No. The calculation runs entirely in your browser, and nothing you enter, including debt names, is sent to a server or saved.
